question: What is the difference between threading and multiprocessing in Python, and when do you use each?
title: Threading vs Multiprocessing in Python
direct_answer: Threading uses multiple threads in the same process sharing memory, but the GIL prevents true parallel CPU execution — only one thread executes Python bytecode at a time. Use threading for I/O-bound tasks (network calls, file I/O) where threads wait and yield the GIL. Use multiprocessing to spawn separate processes, each with its own GIL, for CPU-bound tasks (number crunching, image processing). For I/O-bound at scale, asyncio is usually better than threading.
interviewer_intent: Tests understanding of Python's concurrency model and when each approach applies — a question that separates theoretical knowledge from practical experience.

sections.title: The GIL and its implications
sections.content:
The Global Interpreter Lock (GIL) is a mutex that allows only one thread to execute Python bytecode at a time per process. This makes CPython thread-safe at the interpreter level but means threads cannot run CPU-bound Python code in parallel.

Threads: share memory space, low overhead to create, fast context switching. The GIL is released during I/O operations (network, file, sleep) — so multiple threads can overlap I/O waits efficiently. threading.Thread, ThreadPoolExecutor. Good for: database queries, HTTP calls, file reads, anything that spends time waiting.

Multiprocessing: each Process has its own Python interpreter and GIL. True parallel CPU execution. Higher overhead (spawning a process, serializing arguments with pickle, IPC). multiprocessing.Process, ProcessPoolExecutor. Good for: CPU-intensive computation, image/video processing, scientific computing.

Asyncio: single-threaded but cooperative multitasking via an event loop. You write async/await code; Python switches between coroutines at await points. Scales to thousands of concurrent I/O operations with much less overhead than threading. Best choice for I/O-bound services in modern Python.

sections.title: When to use each
sections.content:
from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor, ProcessPoolExecutor
import threading
import multiprocessing

# I/O-bound: threading or asyncio
import requests
URLs = ['https://api.example.com/user/1', 'https://api.example.com/user/2']

# ThreadPoolExecutor for I/O-bound
with ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=10) as executor:
    results = list(executor.map(requests.get, URLs))

# CPU-bound: multiprocessing
def compute_intensive(n: int) -> int:
    return sum(i*i for i in range(n))  # pure CPU

numbers = [10_000_000] * 4  # 4 tasks

# Single-threaded: sequential (slow for CPU)
results = [compute_intensive(n) for n in numbers]

# ProcessPoolExecutor: true parallelism
with ProcessPoolExecutor(max_workers=4) as executor:
    results = list(executor.map(compute_intensive, numbers))

# Shared state between threads requires locks
counter = 0
lock = threading.Lock()

def increment():
    global counter
    with lock:
        counter += 1  # atomic with lock

# multiprocessing.Value for shared state across processes
shared_count = multiprocessing.Value('i', 0)
shared_lock = multiprocessing.Lock()

sections.title: Concurrency selection rules
items: GIL: threads can't parallelize CPU-bound Python code
I/O-bound: asyncio first (scales best), threading second
CPU-bound: multiprocessing (bypasses GIL via separate processes)
ThreadPoolExecutor / ProcessPoolExecutor: simpler than raw threads/processes
Shared state in threads: use threading.Lock; across processes: multiprocessing.Queue or Value

speakable_v2.hook: The GIL is why threading doesn't help CPU-bound Python — and why asyncio is usually better than threading for I/O.

beats.content: The GIL allows only one thread to execute Python bytecode at a time. For CPU-bound work, threads can't run in parallel — they take turns. Multiprocessing bypasses this by spawning separate processes, each with its own GIL.

For I/O-bound work, threads work because the GIL is released during I/O operations — threads overlap their wait time. But asyncio is usually better: one thread, cooperative multitasking, scales to thousands of concurrent connections.
For CPU-intensive work — number crunching, image processing — use multiprocessing.ProcessPoolExecutor. True parallelism across cores, each process runs independently.

speakable_v2.cap: Quick rule: I/O-bound → asyncio (or threading). CPU-bound → multiprocessing. Never threading for CPU in Python.
speakable_v2.followup_handoff: Follow up with the GIL's implementation, or concurrent.futures for cleaner pool management.
